Regression analysis

Words: 30
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Regression analysis studies how a response variable depends on explanatory variables through a regression model. It estimates that dependence and assesses uncertainty in fitted regression coefficients, predictions and model comparisons. Linear regression is one important case.

Mark and recapture

Words: 183 Articles: 2
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Mark and recapture estimates cardinality or survival from repeated observations after marking and releasing individuals. In the simplest closed-population experiment, overlap between two samples estimates the fraction marked. More elaborate capture-recapture models allow changing survival and detection probabilities.

Capture-recapture model

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Mark and recapture OurBigBook.com
Repeated capture and release observations estimate population or survival characteristics while allowing incomplete detection. In a first-recapture array, mij​ counts individuals released at occasion i and next observed at j. A survival probability ϕj​ and detection probability Pj+1​ contribute a no-observation continuation factor ϕj​(1−Pj+1​). The resulting likelihood depends on both survival and detection; these probabilities need not be separately identifiable at the last observation interval.

Missing-count EM for capture-recapture (E[nij​∣m,ϕ,P]=Ni​wij​/Ci​)

Words: 81
Capture-recapture model OurBigBook.com
Let Ni​=Ri​−∑s=i+1J​mis​ count individuals never recaptured after release i. Partition them into death-interval counts nij​ and terminal survivors niJ​. Their unnormalized weights are wij​=(1−ϕj​)∏ℓ=ij−1​ϕℓ​(1−Pℓ+1​) for j<J, and wiJ​=∏ℓ=iJ−1​ϕℓ​(1−Pℓ+1​). Conditional counts are multinomial with normalizer Ci​=∑j=iJ​wij​. The EM algorithm replaces all missing counts by the displayed conditional expectations, then maximizes the resulting complete-data log likelihood. Survival and detection updates are expected successes divided by expected opportunities. A flat observed-likelihood ridge remains nonidentifiable even if each conditional complete-data maximization is explicit.

Nonlinear regression

Words: 42
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Nonlinear regression fits a conditional mean whose dependence on its parameters is nonlinear. In a normal distribution observation model, the likelihood is based on residuals yi​−m(xi​,θ). Nonlinearity can create parameter trade-offs, asymmetric uncertainty and several posterior regions, so prior predictive checks and Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence diagnostics can be especially useful.

Outlier

Words: 44
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
An outlier is an observation unusually far from the behavior expected under a statistical model. A large regression residual can identify a candidate, but data validation, regression leverage, and the possibility of model misspecification should be examined before excluding it. An outlier need not be an influential observation.

Regression to the mean

Words: 61
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
An unusually extreme noisy observation tends to be followed by a less extreme observation even without intervention. Selecting locations for an intervention because they had high prior event counts can therefore bias a simple before-and-after comparison toward an apparent reduction. The effect follows from conditioning on an extreme value with a transient random component, rather than from a causal treatment effect.

Response variable (Y)

Words: 48
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
A response variable is the outcome whose variation is described by a statistical model or whose change is compared across treatments. Its unit, measurement procedure and observation time must be specified. An outcome consisting of a feature count is one response per sketch, not one independent experimental response per feature.

Scientific control

Words: 49
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
A scientific control supplies a comparison or procedure that distinguishes an intended effect from other influences on an experiment or observational measurement. Negative controls should show no target effect; positive controls should show a known effect. A negative control outcome applies this logic to an outcome that the exposure cannot causally affect.

Design of experiments

Words: 2k Articles: 44
Statistical modelling OurBigBook.com
Design of experiments chooses experimental units, treatments, replication, blocks in experimental design and randomization so that scientifically useful treatment contrasts can be estimated with meaningful standard errors. Allocation determines which measurements supply independent treatment information.

Optimal experimental design

Words: 350 Articles: 6
Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
Optimal experimental design chooses observation locations and allocations to optimize a specified criterion for a specified statistical model. Criteria can control the determinant of an estimator's covariance matrix or its worst prediction variance. Optimality depends on the model and the permitted design class, including whether allocations are integer or approximate.

General equivalence theorem for optimal design

Words: 109
Optimal experimental design OurBigBook.com
For continuous regressors spanning a p-dimensional space on a compact design region, and approximate designs with nonsingular information matrix of an experimental design, the following are equivalent: D-optimal design, G-optimal design, and supx​d(x,ξ)=p. A D-optimal design has nonpositive directional derivatives d(x,ξ)−p. Conversely, if every such derivative is nonpositive, concavity of logdet bounds every competing information matrix by the tangent at M(ξ), proving D-optimality. The sensitivity average is p, and a D-optimal design exists by compactness of the information-matrix set and the spanning assumption; hence the optimal G-value is p. Sensitivity equals p at every support point of an optimal design. The equivalence concerns approximate allocations; integer restrictions can change exact-design optima.

G-optimal design (minξ​supx​d(x,ξ))

Words: 39
Optimal experimental design OurBigBook.com
A G-optimal design minimizes the maximum design sensitivity function over the full design region. Thus it minimizes the worst variance of a fitted regression mean, excluding the separate noise variance of a new observation. The sensitivity average is p, so its supremum is at least p.

D-optimal design (maxξ​detM(ξ))

Words: 34
Optimal experimental design OurBigBook.com
A D-optimal design maximizes the determinant of the information matrix of an experimental design, equivalently minimizing the determinant of the covariance matrix of a fixed-size least-squares estimator. It minimizes the volume of a fixed-level confidence ellipsoid for the model coefficients under the usual Gaussian model.

Approximate experimental design (ξ=∑i​wi​δxi​​)

Words: 125 Articles: 2
Optimal experimental design OurBigBook.com
An approximate design is a probability measure on the design region, with weight wi​ specifying a proportion of observations at xi​. For N independent observations and common error variance σ2, a linear regression with vector f(x) has normalized information matrix of an experimental design M(ξ)=∫f(x)f(x)Tdξ(x); its least-squares estimator has covariance σ2M(ξ)−1/N when the allocations realize these proportions. Exact designs restrict Nwi​ to integers.
Information matrix of an experimental design (M(ξ)=∫f(x)f(x)Tdξ(x))
Words: 72 Articles: 1
Approximate experimental design OurBigBook.com
The normalized information matrix for a homoscedastic linear regression model is the average outer product of its regressor vector. It is positive-definite precisely when the supported regressors span the parameter space. The full Fisher information matrix under normal errors is NM(ξ)/σ2.
Design sensitivity function (d(x,ξ)=f(x)TM(ξ)−1f(x))
Words: 38
Information matrix of an experimental design OurBigBook.com
The sensitivity function is the normalized variance of a fitted regression mean. Its average under the design is the number p of model coefficients, since ∫ddξ=tr(M−1M)=p. The directional derivative of logdetM towards a point mass at x is d(x,ξ)−p.

Latin square

Words: 203 Articles: 3
Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
A Latin square of order q is a q×q array of q symbols, each occurring once in each row and column. Used as a row-column design, its symbols label treatments. Centered treatment indicators are orthogonal to both row and column indicators, because every row-treatment and column-treatment pair occurs once. This balance separates additive effects from two nuisance directions.

Analysis of variance for a Latin square

Words: 72
Latin square OurBigBook.com
For one response per cell in an order-q Latin square, fit an intercept and additive row, column and treatment effects with sum-to-zero constraints. Each factor contributes q−1 statistical degrees of freedom; the residual has q2−1−3(q−1)=(q−1)(q−2). The centered factor spaces are mutually orthogonal, so sequential sums of squares do not depend on fitting order. With an additional orthogonal symbol factor from a Graeco-Latin square, residual statistical degrees of freedom become (q−1)(q−3). Exact F-tests require independent equal-variance normal errors; unmodeled interactions can invalidate the error term.

Mutually orthogonal Latin squares

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Latin square OurBigBook.com
Latin squares on the same array are mutually orthogonal when every ordered pair of symbols from any two squares occurs exactly once on superposition. Pairwise balance makes the centered symbol-indicator spaces orthogonal in an additive linear regression model.
Graeco-Latin square
Words: 43
Mutually orthogonal Latin squares OurBigBook.com
A Graeco-Latin square is the superposition of two orthogonal Latin squares of the same order. Each symbol of either square occurs once per row and column, and every cross-square pair occurs once. It permits four mutually orthogonal additive factor spaces: rows, columns, and the two symbol factors.

Contrast (statistics)

Words: 29
Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
A contrast is a linear combination ∑i​ci​μi​ of group means with ∑i​ci​=0. It compares responses without depending on a common additive level. Treatment contrasts and factorial contrasts specify comparisons in a design of experiments.

Response surface methodology

Words: 347 Articles: 5
Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
Response surface methodology fits local regression approximations to a quantitative response as experimental settings change. A first-order model estimates a local gradient; augmenting the design permits quadratic regression, curvature assessment and local optimization. Extrapolating a fitted surface outside the experimentally supported region requires caution.

Center-point curvature contrast (γ​=YˉF​−Yˉ0​)

Words: 76
Response surface methodology OurBigBook.com
In a two-factor design with four corner observations and n0​ independent center replicates, the difference between the corner mean and center mean has variance σ2(1/4+1/n0​). Under a full quadratic regression surface it estimates β11​+β22​; the linear and interaction terms average to zero at the corners. With n0​≥2, the center pure error estimate makes its squared standardized contrast an F1,n0​−1​ test under a first-order mean model. Zero contrast does not exclude curvature, since the two squared-term coefficients may cancel.

Steepest ascent in response surface methodology (d=b/∥b∥)

Words: 76
Response surface methodology OurBigBook.com
For a fitted local first-order response m(x)=β​0​+bTx, the unit direction maximizing its directional derivative in coded Euclidean distance is d=b/∥b∥, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Run sequential feasible settings x0​+hd, increase h while measured response improves, and refit near promising settings. Physical increments are hj​hdj​, so coded and unscaled physical gradients need not give the same experimental path. A near-zero gradient calls for further modeling rather than division by zero.

Coded experimental variable (xj​=(ξj​−cj​)/hj​)

Words: 42
Response surface methodology OurBigBook.com
A coded experimental variable rescales a physical setting ξj​ around its center cj​, dividing by a chosen positive half-range hj​. The endpoints cj​±hj​ become ±1, giving dimensionless factorial design coordinates. The choice of scale affects the metric used for steepest ascent in response surface methodology.

Rotatable design

Words: 72
Response surface methodology OurBigBook.com
A design for a specified polynomial model is rotatable when the variance of a fitted regression mean depends on a setting only through its distance from the centre. For a full 2d factorial portion plus symmetric axial points in a central composite design, fourth-order rotational symmetry requires ∑xi4​=3∑xi2​xj2​. These sums are 2d+2α4 and 2d, giving α=(2d)1/4. Sign symmetry removes odd moments and equal second moments complete the required moment symmetry for a full quadratic model.

Central composite design

Words: 42
Response surface methodology OurBigBook.com
A central composite design augments a factorial portion with axial points ±αej​ and replicated centre points. It supports a full quadratic response model: intercept, linear terms, cross-products and squared coordinates. Centre-point replication estimates pure error. Choosing the axial distance appropriately gives a rotatable design.

Split-plot design

Words: 52
Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
A split-plot design randomizes one factor to whole plots and another to subplots within each whole plot. Whole-plot treatment effects and subplot treatment effects therefore use different error ANOVA strata. Whole plots provide replication for the first factor; their subplots do not supply extra independent whole-plot replication. Within-whole-plot comparisons can remove a shared additive whole-plot variance component.

Factorial design

Words: 351 Articles: 6
Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
A factorial design includes every combination of specified factor levels. Balanced replication permits separate estimation of marginal effects and interaction terms. The factor allocation, not the number of subsamples, determines the appropriate error term for each effect.

Main effect

Words: 44
Factorial design OurBigBook.com
A main effect compares the mean response at different levels of one factor after averaging over the other factors according to the design. With sign coding, its two-level difference is twice the singleton factorial contrast coefficient. In a fractional factorial design, that coefficient can include aliased higher-order effects.

Factorial contrast (χA​(x)=∏j∈A​xj​)

Words: 58
Factorial design OurBigBook.com
In a two-level factorial design, a factor subset defines a sign column. The coefficient of this column is its response contrast divided by the number of runs when the columns are orthogonal. A singleton describes a main effect and a pair describes a two-factor interaction. On the full cube, distinct columns have zero inner product: summing over any coordinate in their symmetric difference cancels the terms.

Fractional factorial design

Words: 216 Articles: 3
Factorial design OurBigBook.com
A fractional factorial design uses a selected subset of the full factor-level combinations. In a regular two-level fraction, encode levels by signs and impose k independent equations ∏j∈Gi​​xj​=si​. Independence of the generator incidence vectors over F2​ leaves 2m−k runs. Reduced run count creates aliasing in a fractional factorial design, which must be evaluated against the effects scientifically required.
Resolution of a fractional factorial design (R=minG∈H∖{I}​∣G∣)
Words: 47
Fractional factorial design OurBigBook.com
The resolution of a regular fraction is the shortest nonidentity word in its defining contrast subgroup. Two effects alias only when their word product belongs to that subgroup. Thus resolution VI separates all main effects and two-factor interactions from one another and from three-factor interactions, though some three-factor interactions alias in complementary pairs.

Factor subsets multiply by symmetric difference; their sign columns multiply pointwise. The subgroup generated by independent defining words has 2k elements. On a selected fractional factorial design, every word in this subgroup is constant, with sign determined by the chosen generator signs. The cosets classify identical or opposite contrast columns.

Conversely, averaging a character over the fraction vanishes unless its word belongs to the defining contrast subgroup, so every alias class is exactly a subgroup coset. In a half fraction each class has two distinct words; their separate coefficients cannot be identified without assumptions or additional runs.

Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
A crossover design assigns each subject a sequence of treatments in successive periods. Subject blocking can reduce between-subject variation; balanced sequences can separate treatment from period effects. A carryover effect or irreversible change can invalidate a simple within-subject comparison.

A carryover effect is an effect of a previous treatment on a later response. Balanced transitions help prevent a treatment from being preceded disproportionately by one particular alternative, but do not ensure that carryover effects vanish or are separately identifiable in every model.

A completely randomized design assigns treatments directly to available experimental units using complete randomization, without blocking. Fixed group sizes can be enforced. The residual then includes uncontrolled between-unit variation.

Design of experiments OurBigBook.com
A block groups experimental units expected to have similar background responses. Comparing treatments within blocks can reduce the variance of an estimator. Block allocation must be specified before responses are used to evaluate treatment effects.

For a linear regression model Ybj​=αb​+f(xbj​)Tβ+ϵbj​ with one unrestricted intercept per two-run experimental block, differencing the responses removes all experimental block effects. The parameter vector β is identifiable precisely when the matrix whose rows are f(xb1​)−f(xb2​) has full column rank. This criterion applies to arbitrary pairings, including nonregular factorial designs; requiring regular orthogonal confounding is a stronger constraint.

Partition a regular factorial design by fixed signs of independent factorial contrasts. Products of those block-generating columns span the block effects. A treatment contrast that is constant on each block is therefore confounded with block differences. Select generators so that only scientifically dispensable treatment effects enter this space; randomize the assignment of blocks and the run order within each block.

A block design assigns treatments to experimental units partitioned into blocks. Its incidence counts nij​ record how often treatment i occurs in block j. Balance and connectedness determine which treatment contrasts are estimable and how much adjustment for blocks costs.

A binary block design has t treatments, b blocks of size k<t, every treatment in r blocks, and every distinct pair in λ blocks. Counting occurrences and pairs gives tr=bk and r(k−1)=λ(t−1). Its incidence matrix of a set system N satisfies NNT=(r−λ)I+λ11T. For statistical comparison of all treatment effects one also needs connectedness; λ>0 guarantees it, whereas singleton blocks with λ=0 do not.

A balanced incomplete block design is symmetric when its number of blocks equals its number of treatments. The identity bk=tr then gives r=k. Its square incidence matrix of a set system N obeys NNT=(r−λ)I+λJ, with eigenvalues r−λ of multiplicity t−1 and r2 of multiplicity one.

For every prime, the exponent in the left side is even and that in r2 is even, so its exponent in r−λ must be even. Thus r−λ is a perfect square. A row-column design has two crossed partitions of experimental units into rows and columns. A randomized complete block design places every treatment in every block, with a common replication pattern, and uses independent within-block randomization. Such equal-proportion designs are orthogonal block designs.

Block design OurBigBook.com
An orthogonal block design has centered treatment-indicator vectors orthogonal to centered block-indicator vectors on the experimental units. Fitting by the check loss uses an asymmetric absolute-error penalty, so different values of τ describe different parts of the response distribution. If the conditional error distribution function is continuous and strictly increasing with τ-quantile zero, the conditional expected check loss is uniquely minimized at zero fitted displacement. If every incorrect parameter differs from the true regression function on an event of positive probability, averaging these nonnegative conditional risk differences gives strict identifiability of the true parameter. Integrable errors and bounded regression functions supply finite risks.

The check loss weights positive errors by τ and negative errors by 1−τ. It is convex, continuous and Lipschitz with constant max(τ,1−τ). At τ=1/2 it is half the absolute error. Its expected value elicits a quantile: asymmetry determines which probability level the fitted location targets.

Bounded difference quotients justify differentiation by dominated convergence. Integrating the derivative between the unique quantile and another location proves strict optimality. Edge log-ratios are independent real coordinates and each binomial log-likelihood term is strictly concave, proving existence and uniqueness of the normalized estimate. If that comparison graph is a connected graph and the abilities are finite, the quadratic form vanishes only for constant vectors. Words: 418 Articles: 6
Latent variable OurBigBook.com
The expectation-maximization algorithm alternates an E-step, which takes the conditional expectation of a complete-data log objective over latent variables, and an M-step, which maximizes that expected objective over the parameters.

Words: 97
Expectation-maximization algorithm OurBigBook.com
For N observations from each of two labeled exponential distributions, an E-step may produce positive completed time totals U,V. Its expected complete-data log-likelihood is Q=Nlogλ1​+Nlogλ2​−Uλ1​−Vλ2​. This is strictly concave. On the closed ordering constraint λ1​≥λ2​>0, its maximum is (N/U,N/V) when U<V; otherwise it lies at λ1​=λ2​=2N/(U+V). To see the boundary case, first maximize along the equality line. At that maximum, moving into either feasible rate-separating direction has directional derivative (V−U)/2≤0, so concavity proves global optimality. For the open constraint λ1​>λ2​, this boundary value is a supremum rather than an attained M-step.

For a multinomial distribution with two unobserved cells merged into one observed count, the conditional allocation is a binomial distribution with probabilities proportional to the two cell probabilities. The expectation-maximization algorithm replaces the missing counts by their conditional expectations in the parameter-dependent part of the complete-data log-likelihood. The expectation of a log-factorial normalization generally differs from its value at the expected count, but this difference is independent of the candidate parameter and does not affect the maximization step.

Words: 74
Expectation-maximization algorithm OurBigBook.com
For independent normal coordinates, an unobserved first coordinate has conditional law equal to its current marginal normal distribution, even when the second coordinate of that observation is known. Thus its E-step first moment is μ1(t)​ and second moment is (μ1(t)​)2+v1(t)​. With three observed first coordinates and one missing value, the mean update is (∑i=13​xi1​+μ1(t)​)/4 and the variance update is [∑i=13​(xi1​−μ1(t+1)​)2+v1(t)​+(μ1(t)​−μ1(t+1)​)2]/4. The conditional variance term is essential: filling in only the conditional mean is not the expectation-maximization algorithm.

The expectation-maximization algorithm maximizes ∑a,b​Nab​logKab​ over row probability distributions, giving Kabnew​=Nab​/∑c​Nac​. A row with zero total count is unrestricted by this objective. Belief propagation computes the counts exactly on a tree.

The M-step maximizes the expected stationary complete-data log-likelihood, including the initial-observation density and the conditional-variance contribution to the two adjacent innovation squares.

Quasi-complete separation occurs when a nonzero direction d makes all these margins nonnegative, with some zero and some strictly positive. Cochran's theorem OurBigBook.com
Let Ai​ be real symmetric matrices with sum In​. Their matrix ranks sum to at least n, because their ranges span Rn. If the ranks sum to n, those ranges form a direct sum. For y in the range of Ai​, the identity y=∑j​Aj​y and uniqueness of its range decomposition imply Aj​y=δij​y. Thus Ai2​=Ai​ and Ai​Aj​=0 for i=j: the matrices are mutually orthogonal orthogonal projections. In a combined orthonormal basis, the forms ZTAi​Z for Z∼Nn​(0,In​) use disjoint sets of independent standard normal coordinates. They are independent chi-squared distributions with degrees of freedom equal to the ranks. Conversely, if all these forms have those chi-squared laws, their expectations and their sum give ∑i​rankAi​=n.

Bayes' theorem gives the conditional probabilities r1​=P(A∣G)=aq/p and r0​=P(A∣Gc)=(1−a)q/(1−p). Their risk ratio is the displayed expression: the unknown overall selection probability cancels. Equivalently, it is the ratio of the group-membership odds after selection to those before selection.
When both selection probabilities lie strictly between zero and one, the selection odds ratio is [r1​/(1−r1​)]/[r0​/(1−r0​)] and generally depends on q. Thus compositions alone do not identify that odds ratio or provide sample sizes for a standard error. When a<p, the first group's observed selection rate is lower; this comparison alone does not establish a causal effect of group membership.

Conversely, if the modified count is r and both original values meet the rank-r threshold, reinserting them leaves at least r qualifying values. Different conventions call either of these a correction factor, so the normalization should always be stated explicitly.
Bartlett correction for a normal variance with unknown mean (b=11/6)
Words: 62
Bartlett correction coefficient OurBigBook.com
For a sample of size n≥2 from a normal distribution with unknown mean, the null variance likelihood-ratio test statistic is W=n[−log(U/n)+U/n−1], where U∼χn−12​. With V=(U−n)/n, its expected Taylor terms start with n[EV2/2−EV3/3+EV4/4]. Here EV2=(2n−1)/n2, EV3=(2n−3)/n3, and EV4=(12n2+4n−15)/n4. Higher fixed-order terms contribute only O(n−2) under valid termwise asymptotic integration. Thus E0​W=1+11/(6n)+O(n−2) and WB​=W/[1+11/(6n)].

Likelihood-ratio test of area-proportional Poisson means (Λ=(3S1​/T)S1​(3S2​/(2T))S2​)
Words: 72
Generalized likelihood-ratio test OurBigBook.com
Two equally numerous groups of independent counts with Poisson distributions have areas a and 2a. Under common density their group means are in ratio 1:2. With group sums S1​,S2​ and T=S1​+S2​, the maximized alternative-to-null likelihood ratio is
Λ=(3S1​/T)S1​(3S2​/(2T))S2​.
(100)
Use zero-count limits and Λ=1 when T=0. The regular Wilks theorem calibration has one degree of freedom. Exactly conditioning on T gives S1​∼Binomial(T,1/3) under the null; this supports small-count testing without the large-sample approximation.

D=2{ℓsat​−ℓfit​}.

Residual deviance (D=2ϕ{ℓsaturated​(ϕ)−ℓfitted​(ϕ)})
Words: 141 Articles: 1
Analysis of deviance for nested generalized linear models OurBigBook.com
The unscaled residual deviance of an exponential dispersion family compares its fitted mean with the saturated statistical model at a common dispersion parameter. Its normalization removes the factor 1/ϕ in the log-likelihood. In Poisson regression and binomial regression, ϕ=1, so it is twice the saturated-minus-fitted log-likelihood. Under suitable regularity, D/ϕ has approximately a chi-squared distribution with the residual degrees of freedom; this is not an automatic accurate approximation for sparse responses. Nested deviance reductions with estimated dispersion lead to approximate F-tests after scaling by the dispersion estimate.
Null deviance (D0​=2ϕ[ℓsaturated​−ℓintercept​])
Words: 69
Residual deviance OurBigBook.com
The null deviance is the unscaled deviance of the intercept-only mean model relative to the saturated model at a common dispersion parameter ϕ, retaining any known generalized linear model offset. It supplies a baseline against which predictor terms improve the fit. Its difference from a fitted model's residual deviance, divided by ϕ, is the statistic for a likelihood-ratio test of those added terms, with nuisance parameters handled consistently in both fits. In Poisson and binomial families, ϕ=1.

Most powerful test for a Laplace location shift (X>cα​)

Words: 59
Neyman-Pearson lemma OurBigBook.com
For two unit-scale Laplace distributions with locations θ0​<θ1​, the likelihood ratio is nondecreasing in X, with constant tails and an increasing middle interval. Therefore an upper-tail statistical test of exact size of a statistical test α is a most powerful test. Its cutoff is cα​=θ0​−log(2α) for α≤1/2, and cα​=θ0​+log(2(1−α)) otherwise. Under location θ1​, its statistical power is 21​eθ1​−cα​ if cα​≥θ1​, and 1−21​ecα​−θ1​ otherwise. Constant likelihood ratio tails can make the most powerful test nonunique.

Minimum sum of errors in a simple hypothesis test (C={f1​>f0​},min(α+β)=∫min(f0​,f1​))

Words: 56
Neyman-Pearson lemma OurBigBook.com
For two simple hypotheses with probability densities f0​,f1​, a critical region C has sum of Type I error and Type II error probabilities ∫C​f0​+∫Cc​f1​. Pointwise minimization chooses C={f1​>f0​}, with either decision allowed on the equality set. Thus the optimal likelihood ratio threshold is 1, and the minimum is ∫min(f0​,f1​)=1−21​∫∣f1​−f0​∣. This criterion weights the two error probabilities equally; unequal costs or prior probabilities change the threshold.

Exponential-rate likelihood-ratio test (β(λ)=1−e−λc∑j=0n−1​(λc)j/j!)

Words: 66
Neyman-Pearson lemma OurBigBook.com
For independent exponential distribution observations with rate λ, the likelihood ratio for a larger simple rate is decreasing in their sum. The Neyman-Pearson lemma therefore selects a lower-tail sum threshold c. The sum has a gamma distribution, giving the displayed power; its derivative is ce−λc(λc)n−1/(n−1)!>0. Calibrating at λ0​ gives size α for the composite null λ≤λ0​ and a uniformly most powerful test against larger rates.

Uniformly most powerful test for an exponential rate

Words: 55
Neyman-Pearson lemma OurBigBook.com
For independent samples from an exponential distribution, a test of rate at most λ0​ against rate greater than λ0​ rejects for small sample sums. All simple-alternative likelihood ratios against λ0​ decrease with that sum; its gamma distribution calibrates the size at λ0​. Monotonicity of the rejection probability in the rate proves that this is a uniformly most powerful test for the composite hypotheses.

Monotone likelihood ratio

Words: 287 Articles: 4
Neyman-Pearson lemma OurBigBook.com
A one-parameter family has a monotone likelihood ratio in a statistic T when f(x∣θ1​)/f(x∣θ0​) is nondecreasing in T(x) whenever θ1​>θ0​.
Posterior odds are monotone under a monotone likelihood ratio
Words: 100
Monotone likelihood ratio OurBigBook.com
For a family with a monotone likelihood ratio in T, a prior density π and cutoff a, the posterior odds of θ>a against θ≤a are nondecreasing in T. To prove it, write the unnormalized masses as A(t) and B(t). For t2​>t1​, the difference A(t2​)B(t1​)−A(t1​)B(t2​) is the double integral over θ>a≥η of π(θ)π(η)[fθ​(t2​)fη​(t1​)−fθ​(t1​)fη​(t2​)]. Each integrand is nonnegative by the likelihood-ratio ordering. Common factors in the full-data likelihood cancel from the odds, so the same argument works when T is a statistic rather than the complete observation. Interpret zero denominators by extended odds whenever the posterior is defined.
Monotone test
Words: 127
Monotone likelihood ratio OurBigBook.com
An upper-tail monotone test in a real statistic T has rejection probability ϕ=1T>c​+η1T=c​, with 0≤η≤1; the constant tests correspond to infinite cutoffs. For a family with positive densities on a common support and a monotone likelihood ratio in T, its power function can cross that of an arbitrary competing test only from below to above as the parameter increases. If r=fθ1​​/fθ0​​ and θ1​>θ0​, choose a positive number k between the ratios on opposite sides of the cutoff. The signs of ϕ−ϕ′ and r−k agree away from T=c, and r=k at a boundary with positive mass. Therefore Eθ1​​(ϕ−ϕ′)≥kEθ0​​(ϕ−ϕ′). In particular strict positivity at θ0​ propagates to θ1​. Positivity of the densities matters for this strict conclusion; with changing supports only a weak conclusion may remain.
